label: t4-glide-alt
summary: Keep the whirling-fruit system as the main Track 4 build, and run the ballasted plate glider alongside it. The fruit gives a pre-build number and public data, but it is a vertical sink with no forward glide, so the accepted glide-range law (x <= h*(L/D)max) gives a bound of 0 m and cannot test it. The plate glider (L/D 3.77 recomputed, paper 3.8) engages that law and the ground-effect and wind-glide laws, and needs only a long channel. Six alternatives are laid out in the table (plate, printed samara with LEV model, flying-fish fin models, humidity-folding glider, Draco lizard data, flying snake) plus two same-variable neighbour studies. The strongest rival explanation is the leading-edge-vortex lift account (Lentink 2009; Jung and Rezgui 2023, 2026), which differs from the chosen model only in how lift is closed (explicit LEV lift forms vs a fitted curve); a third account (separated vortex ring, Liu 2025) is for a different seed. Cheapest extra arm: fit a normal-force LEV model to the public fruit data; whether its code is public was not checked. Law set 1.8.1 differs from 1.6.0 by six non-flight laws; the flight laws are unchanged and the four flight gaps remain proposed.
lay_summary: The main experiment drops small 3D-printed seed-pods, shaped like maple helicopters, through water and asks which wing curve makes them fall slowest. These pods only spin and sink, so they never glide sideways, and our rule about how far a glider can travel has nothing to say about them. A flat plate with a weight at its front is a cheap second experiment: slide the weight and the plate flutters, glides or dives, like a paper plane. Other options are fish-fin models, a lizard that really glides in the wild, and a fold-up seed glider that bends with damp air. Scientists disagree on why spinning seeds fall slowly: one account says a small tornado of air stuck to the wing lifts it, the other fits a simple curve to measurements. We recommend keeping the seed-pod test and adding the plate test next to it.

findings.claim: The chosen system (Fauli, Rabault, Carlson) says its own model is a minimal blade-element theory and that a strong leading-edge vortex exists at its Reynolds numbers; the vortex enters only through the shape of the lift and drag curves, not through a vortex model.
findings.evidence_quote: experiments and simulations at Reynolds numbers comparable to the ones we experience indicate the existence of a strong leading edge vortex, that changes the stall pattern compared with higher Reynolds number

findings.claim: The chosen system names the plain disk-loading rule as the textbook baseline: descent speed goes as the square root of mass over swept disk area.
findings.evidence_quote: descent velocity is proportional to the square-root of the wing-loading, i.e., its mass divided by the disk defined by the projected wing area during rotation

findings.claim: The chosen system explains the optimal fold angle with an energy-limited-sepal argument plus hydrodynamic theory (the letter).
findings.evidence_quote: Both hydrodynamic theory and experiments involving synthetic, double-winged fruits show that to produce a maximal flight time there is an optimal fold angle for the desiccated sepals.

findings.claim: Strongest competing explanation: the slow descent of autorotating seeds is produced by a stable leading-edge vortex (LEV) that raises lift, as shown on a robot seed with 3-D flow measurement (Lentink et al. 2009).
findings.evidence_quote: Maple seeds and a hornbeam seed create a prominent leading-edge vortex that is similar to the flow structures that are responsible for the high lift generated by the wings of hovering insects and bats.

findings.claim: A rival blade-element model for the same kind of body replaces the fitted lift curve with explicit LEV lift forms (normal-force or Polhamus) and is validated on wind-tunnel data from three sycamore seeds; the normal-force form is preferred.
findings.evidence_quote: both the normal force and Polhamus lift models combined with the normal force drag can be used to describe the two-dimensional lift characteristics of a samara exhibiting an LEV.

findings.claim: Earlier LEV-lift blade-element model (Polhamus-based sectional lift) agreed with wind-tunnel rotation speed and descent rate for a samara wing.
findings.evidence_quote: The results showed good agreement between the numerical model and the experimental measurements of rotational speed and rate of descent of the samara wing.

findings.claim: A 2026 follow-up (Jung and Rezgui, J. Aircraft) extends the LEV-informed blade-element-momentum model across wind speeds and pitch settings on maple seeds.
findings.evidence_quote: The model demonstrates good agreement across a wide range of flow velocities and pitch settings.

findings.claim: A different mechanism is proposed for a multi-winged seed: a stable separated vortex ring, not the LEV, dominates stable autorotation; fewer wings give larger wing loading and faster stable descent.
findings.evidence_quote: A stable separated vortex ring dominates the stable autorotation of tristellateia seeds.

findings.claim: Fold angle and wing flexibility of origami winged fruits have been studied by a different group (Cai, Hsu, Yen 2024). Only the title and DOI could be read; no abstract is available, so no result is claimed.
Alternative 1, ballasted plate glider: moving the centre of mass moves the plate from flutter and tumble to steady glide to dive. The model is a quasi-steady fit and the paper is open on arXiv.
findings.evidence_quote: Periodic modes such as fluttering, tumbling and bounding give way to steady gliding and then downward diving as the CoM is increasingly displaced towards one edge.

findings.claim: Pomerenk and Ristroph state the plate model peaks at glide ratio 3.8 near centre-of-equilibrium offset 0.22 chord (symbols dropped by text extraction); stable gliding at low mass lies roughly in [0.1, 0.3].
findings.evidence_quote: i.e., around the quarter-chord point (Li et al. 2022).

findings.claim: My re-run of the earlier scout script with the published coefficients gives glide ratio 3.77 at offset 0.218-0.22 chord, glide angle 14.9 deg, and no glide equilibrium at 0.30 or more.

By the registry glide-range bound x <= h*(L/D)max, a plate with L/D 3.77 released 1.2 m up can travel horizontally at most 4.52 m, 18 times the 0.25 m width of the Fauli tank; a plate arm therefore needs a long channel or air, not the existing tank. (0.25 m width taken from the earlier scout report, not re-read.)
Alternative 2, 3-D printed maple samaras (Nave et al. 2021): printed replicas matched natural lab behaviour within one standard deviation; printed on an Ultimaker 3 in PLA.
findings.evidence_quote: We show that the artificial samaras are able to replicate (within one standard deviation) the behavior of natural samaras in a lab setting.

findings.claim: Nave et al. print material and density.
findings.evidence_quote: We used an Ultimaker 3 3D printer with PLA (polylactic acid) as filament, which has a density of 1.24

findings.claim: Alternative 2b: an artificial samara glider design was presented as a poster (Carroll 2023), CC BY 4.0, one 4.5 MB PDF on Zenodo. It is design-level, not a dataset.
findings.evidence_quote: A miniature biomimetic glider inspired by the maple samara was developed to study the flight dynamics of autorotating bodies

findings.claim: Alternative 3, flying-fish wind-tunnel model: pelvic fins raise lift and lift-to-drag ratio and add longitudinal stability (Park and Choi 2010). Publisher full text was not read; abstract only.
findings.evidence_quote: The role of the pelvic fins was found to increase the lift force and lift-to-drag ratio, which is confirmed by the jet-like flow structure existing between the pectoral and pelvic fins.

findings.claim: A modular robotic flying-fish model puts fin position and pitch on a dial: efficiency is best with pelvic fins directly behind the pectoral fins; stability and lift trade off (Reynolds 30,000).
findings.evidence_quote: Results show that the aerodynamic efficiency is maximized for pelvic fins located directly behind the pectoral fins and is higher for more positive pitch angles.

findings.claim: CFD on a flying-fish body gives a maximum lift-to-drag ratio of 4.7 (Deng et al. 2019); it is a simulation of the Park-Choi model, not an independent measurement.
findings.evidence_quote: the maximum lift-to-drag ratio of 4.7 is achieved at

findings.claim: Alternative 4, humidity-actuated Alsomitra-type glider (Wiesemuller et al. 2022, CC BY): wing shape self-folds with humidity, design space explored numerically, validated by experiment, two gliding behaviours seen.
findings.evidence_quote: The design space of these gliders is explored and their behavior studied numerically, which allows us to make predictions on their flight characteristics.

findings.claim: Alternative 4b: Cranfield CFD data (CC BY 4.0, 2026) on five Alsomitra-like cross-sections; only two of five reached trimmed gliding. Simulation, no physical build.
findings.evidence_quote: only the Fauvel and Javan Cucumber configurations produced conditions representative of trimmed gliding flight.

findings.claim: Alternative 5, wild gliding lizards (Draco dussumieri) in a seven-camera motion-capture arena; public MATLAB data set is CC BY 4.0, 6,168,372-byte .mat file plus 7,138-byte readme and a 43,342-byte analysis script (figshare listing).
findings.evidence_quote: wild gliding lizards (Draco dussumieri) in a seven-camera motion capture arena

findings.claim: Alternative 6, flying snake (body as wing): quasi-steady theory under-predicts lift by 35% and over-predicts drag by 40% (Yeaton et al. 2024). A cautionary result for any quasi-steady glide model, including the plate model.
findings.evidence_quote: We found that quasi-steady aerodynamic theory under-predicts lift by 35% and over-predicts drag by 40%.

findings.claim: Wild-fruit Reynolds numbers in Fauli Table I are reproduced by Re = U*L/nu with nu = 1.5e-5 m2/s: 2800, 5667, 12800 against paper 2800, 5700, 12700. This confirms the table reading and the air viscosity used.

Law library check: lawset 1.8.1 pins 59 laws and 1.6.0 pins 53; six are new and none is flight-related (development-growth-asymptote, fisher-kpp-speed, kimura-heterozygosity, maynardsmith-hawk-dove, turing-ddi, test-loop-only-density-sanity). Flight laws flight-climb-glide-law, flight-allometry-law, perturb-wind-glide, perturb-isa-vmin have identical content hashes; scaling-area-law moved 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 (hash changed; I did not diff its text). The four flight gaps aspect-ratio-induced-drag, taxiing-thrust, elastic-similarity, fin-length-ratio are still proposed.

Consequence for the chosen system: a vertical autorotating sink has no steady horizontal glide, so the accepted glide-range law gives a bound of 0 m and says nothing about descent speed; only the disk-loading style speed-floor law applies. The plate glider, with L/D near 3.8, engages the glide-range, ground-effect and wind-glide laws directly. (My reasoning from the law statements in the earlier laws-glide report; not a Lean run.)

Earlier design agent reported that on public data the blade-element model underestimates the base-angle effect: psi=0 over psi=35 speed ratio 1.50 measured vs 1.22 from the model. I did not re-derive this; it is why a rival LEV-form model is worth fitting to the same data.

key_claims.claim: The strongest competing explanation for slow autorotating descent is a stable leading-edge vortex raising lift (Lentink 2009), now implemented as explicit LEV lift forms in blade-element models (Jung and Rezgui 2023, 2026); the chosen model captures the vortex only through its fitted lift/drag curve.
key_claims.evidence_quote: both the normal force and Polhamus lift models combined with the normal force drag can be used to describe the two-dimensional lift characteristics of a samara exhibiting an LEV.

key_claims.claim: The plate glider peaks near L/D 3.8 at about 0.22 chord (paper) / 3.77 at 0.218 (my re-run), so a release height h gives at most h*3.77 horizontal range; 1.2 m gives 4.52 m, far beyond the 0.25 m Fauli tank width, so it needs a different rig.
key_claims.evidence_quote: i.e., around the quarter-chord point (Li et al. 2022).

key_claims.claim: A vertical autorotating sink has no steady forward glide, so the accepted glide-range law is vacuous for the chosen system, which is why a gliding alternative should run alongside it.
Law set 1.8.1 adds six non-flight laws to 1.6.0 and leaves the flight laws unchanged (same content hashes); the four flight gaps stay proposed.

Rule 3: D: had 9.4 GB free and C: 5.6 GB at start (df), above thresholds; only a 7 KB file was downloaded. Existing data folder totals 482 MB from other agents (over the 300 MB total cap, not mine); I added no large data.
No Lean run, no OpenAlex, no [held-out clade]/[held-out clade] material used (holdout rule).
recommendations: KEEP the whirling-fruit system as the primary Track 4 build: it is the only candidate with a stored pre-build prediction, a permissive licence and a cheap rig.

RUN ALONGSIDE: the ballasted plate glider (ALT 1), in a channel at least 4.5 m long or in air (arithmetic in law_engagement.py). It is the only option here that uses the accepted glide-range, ground-effect and wind-glide laws and the missing aspect-ratio-drag and stability laws.

ADD AT ZERO BUILD COST: fit an explicit LEV (normal-force) lift model to the same public fruit data and report both models against the same runs, so the rival explanation is tested rather than just cited. First check whether Jung-Rezgui code or data is public (not verified).
DEFER: flying-fish robot (needs wind tunnel and force balance, Re 30,000, no CAD found) until a fish-specific claim must be tested; use Draco data only as a sanity check on L/D claims.
CAUTION: the snake result (quasi-steady error 35% lift, 40% drag) means any quasi-steady plate prediction should be given a wide tolerance until measured.
Re-map laws against 1.8.1, not 1.6.0: no flight law changed, but scaling-area-law is 1.1.0 and should be re-read before citing.

a small spinning tube of air that stays attached along the front edge of a wing and adds lift.
two simple formulas for the extra lift a leading-edge vortex gives.
how far a glider travels sideways for each unit it drops.
a single number comparing push of the flow to stickiness of the fluid; equal numbers mean a model behaves like the real thing.
treating the air force at each moment as if the motion were frozen.
how strongly a wing is curved along its length.
